note.question: How can deep reinforcement learning support sequential targeting?
note.overview: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has opened up many unprecedented opportunities in revolutionizing the digital marketing field. In this study, we designed a DRL-based personalized targeting strategy in a sequential setting. The paper shows that the strategy is able to address three important challenges of sequential targeting: (1) forward looking (balancing between a firm’s current revenue and future revenues), (2) earning while learning (maximizing profits while continuously learning through exploration-exploitation), and (3) scalability (coping with a high-dimensional state and policy space).

In this study, we designed a DRL-based personalized targeting strategy in a sequential setting. The paper shows that the strategy is able to address three important challenges of sequential targeting: (1) forward looking (balancing between a firm’s current revenue and future revenues), (2) earning while learning (maximizing profits while continuously learning through exploration-exploitation), and (3) scalability (coping with a high-dimensional state and policy space).

source.quote: We show that the strategy is able to address three important challenges of sequential targeting: (1) forward looking (balancing between a firm’s current revenue and future revenues), (2) earning while learning (maximizing profits while continuously learning through exploration-exploitation), and (3) scalability (coping with a high-dimensional state and policy space).
We illustrate this through a novel design of a DRL-based artificial intelligence (AI) agent.
To better adapt DRL to complex consumer behavior dimensions, we proposed a quantization-based uncertainty learning heuristic for efficient exploration-exploitation.

Further, in order to better understand the potential underlying mechanisms, we conducted multiple interpretability analyses to explain the patterns of learned optimal policy at both the individual and population levels.
To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to apply DRL to solve the problem of sequential promotions in marketing to maximize long-term platform revenue.

Part 1: Consumer Behavior Simulator The consumer behavior simulator is an important com­ ponent of our framework because we can observe con­ sumer responses only under the finite combination of specific states and actions in historical data.

conditions: When we look at the beginning stage of the promotions from day 1 to day 4, the strict two-cycle alternation policy performs the worst, leading to lower revenues than the DRL-learned optimal policy and the policy using price promotions all the time.
Specifically, we observed that most consumers received consecutive price promotions in the first few days.

After day 4, most people started to have a nonpromotion period between every two price promotions, and the nonpromotion periods gradually became longer because we observed that the proportion of promoted users decreased over time.
